whatItDoes: Calculates net worth by subtracting total liabilities (mortgage, loans, cards) from total assets (cash, home, investments, retirement).
whyItExists: Net worth is the single clearest snapshot of financial position — everything you own minus everything you owe. A quick total makes progress measurable from year to year.
whoShouldUse: Individuals tracking wealth, couples planning finances, and anyone taking stock before a major financial decision.
useCases: Measure total wealth at a single point in time
Review a baseline and track progress over years
See whether a large planned purchase fits the balance sheet
Understand how liabilities compare to assets
Set a yearly net-worth goal and monitor the trend
Evaluate the impact of paying down debt on overall wealth
instructions: Read the net worth and the breakdown
Use current market values, not purchase prices
Re-calculate at the same date each year to track the trend
Add or remove asset/liability lines to model a planned purchase
examples: Paying $20,000 off a card lifts net worth by $20,000 even without any new savings
bestPractices: Use fair current market values, not purchase prices
Include all major assets and every liability
Calculate at a fixed date each year for comparability
Recompute after major events like a home purchase, refinance, or big payoff
commonMistakes: Valuing your home at purchase price instead of market value
Forgetting credit card, auto, or student loans
Leaving out retirement and brokerage accounts from assets
Treating net worth as the only measure of financial health
Ignoring taxes on retirement accounts, which reduce their real value
faq: What counts as an asset? — Cash, savings, the market value of your home, and investments.
What counts as a liability? — Mortgages, auto and student loans, and card balances.
Is a negative net worth bad? — Not always; many people start with student debt, for example.
Is my data shared? — No, everything runs locally in your browser.
Should I count my primary home? — Yes, at fair market value minus the outstanding mortgage.
How often should I track it? — Once a year is enough to see the trend; more often creates noise from market swings.
